Embedding-based retrieval works by mapping queries and documents into a shared vector space, then using geometric proximity as a proxy for relevance — but this proxy breaks down when the query vocabulary comes from a different distribution than the corpus it was trained on. The central question is: under what conditions does a dense retrieval model silently return confidently-wrong neighbors, meaning high-cosine-similarity documents that are semantically off-target relative to the actual information need? Domain shift is the crux: an embedder trained on web text or MS MARCO will have learned associations between tokens that simply don't hold in, say, clinical notes, semiconductor fab logs, or legal discovery corpora — so "elevated troponin" and "elevated privileges" may land closer together than a clinician would ever expect. What beginners miss is that the failure is silent — BM25 will return nothing or low-scored results when vocabulary is absent, giving a clear signal; dense retrieval instead returns something plausible-looking at whatever similarity score fills the top-k, and the downstream LLM has no mechanism to distinguish a true retrieval hit from a hallucinated-proximity artifact. The expert worry is therefore less about recall gaps and more about calibration of the retrieval confidence signal: when does cosine similarity stop being a reliable ordinal ranking of relevance, and how far into the ranked list has it already become noise before any reranker or generator sees it?

The measurable property that degrades is the anisotropy of the embedding distribution — in-domain, a well-trained encoder spreads representations across the hypersphere such that cosine similarity discriminates meaningfully, but under domain shift the target-domain documents collapse into a narrow cone, making nearly all pairwise cosine similarities high and the ranking signal flat. This was quantified rigorously in Ethayarajh (2019) "How Contextual are Contextualized Word Representations?" which showed that upper BERT layers exhibit extreme anisotropy even in-domain, with average cosine similarity between random token pairs exceeding 0.99 in some settings — domain shift makes this worse by pulling the entire document distribution toward a region of the space the encoder never learned to spread out. A second detectable property is intrinsic dimensionality (ID) of the corpus embedding cloud: tools like TwoNN or the sklearn-compatible skdim library can estimate ID without labels, and a sharp drop in ID relative to the encoder's training-domain baseline signals that documents are clustering into a degenerate low-dimensional manifold rather than occupying the representational space the model intended. You can also monitor neighborhood overlap instability: embed a held-out query set, perturb each query with minor paraphrases (synonym substitution, passivization), and measure how much the top-k neighbors change — a stable retrieval space should give Jaccard overlap above ~0.7 for near-paraphrase queries, and scores well below that reveal that small surface changes are crossing implicit decision boundaries, a hallmark of a miscalibrated space. Finally, retrieval score distribution statistics are a cheap proxy: in a healthy system, the gap between rank-1 and rank-10 cosine scores is meaningfully large (often 0.05–0.15 on normalized embeddings); when that gap collapses below ~0.02 across the corpus, you're operating in a regime where the top-k is essentially arbitrary.

The evidence is sobering: naive continued pre-training (MLM or autoregressive) on unlabeled target-domain text largely shifts the cone rather than spreading it — the model learns new token co-occurrence statistics but the contrastive geometry that makes retrieval work is not recovered, because MLM loss has no objective that pushes apart semantically distinct documents. Gao et al. (2022) in the Contriever paper demonstrated this directly: a model continued-pretrained with MLM on biomedical text showed only marginal BEIR improvement on TREC-COVID versus the general-domain baseline, while the same corpus used for unsupervised contrastive pre-training (random cropping as positive pairs) recovered meaningful retrieval geometry — suggesting the loss function, not the data distribution, is the binding constraint. The mechanism is that contrastive objectives (SimCSE, Contriever-style ICT, co-condenser) force the encoder to use its full representational capacity to discriminate between documents in the batch, which hydraulically pressures the distribution toward isotropy; without that pressure, gradient updates from MLM will happily represent domain vocabulary while leaving the angular structure of the embedding space essentially untouched. Quantitatively, Izacard et al. (Contriever, 2022) showed that unsupervised contrastive training on target-domain text with as few as 100K documents recovered nDCG@10 within ~3-5 points of supervised fine-tuning on several BEIR domains, whereas MLM-only adaptation rarely closed more than 1-2 points of the gap. The practical implication is sharp: if you have unlabeled target-domain text and no relevance labels, you should be running unsupervised contrastive adaptation (random span cropping, IDF-weighted sampling, or ICT) rather than continued MLM — and you should instrument intrinsic dimensionality before and after to verify the geometry actually changed, not just the vocabulary alignment.

Yes, standard in-batch negative sampling fails systematically in high-similarity domains, and the failure mode has a precise name: false negative contamination, where documents that are actually relevant to the query appear as negatives simply because they weren't designated as the positive pair — in a corpus of 10,000 nearly-identical legal clauses, any random in-batch negative has meaningful probability of being a true positive, and the contrastive loss then actively penalizes the encoder for correctly recognizing semantic similarity. Robinson et al. (2021) "Contrastive Learning with Hard Negative Samples" showed that as domain homogeneity increases, the fraction of false negatives in standard in-batch sampling can exceed 30-40% in specialized corpora, and that training on such contaminated negatives produces encoders with systematically compressed similarity ranges — exactly the degenerate geometry we're trying to escape. The downstream retrieval consequence is insidious: the encoder learns to artificially deflate similarity scores between semantically close documents to satisfy the loss, meaning that at inference time, the true top-1 document for a precision-critical query (e.g., "find the indemnification clause that excludes gross negligence") may rank below clauses that are superficially different but topically adjacent, because the model was punished during training for bringing them close. ANCE (Xiong et al., 2021) partially addressed this with asynchronous hard negative mining from the index itself, but ANCE assumes you have some labeled anchors to initialize the mining loop — in purely unsupervised adaptation to a new legal or clinical domain, you have no such anchors, so the mining process has no signal to distinguish hard-true-negatives from hard-false-negatives. The practical ceiling here is that retrieval precision in high-homogeneity domains is bounded not by model capacity but by the quality of the negative sampling strategy, and no amount of encoder scaling escapes this if the training signal is corrupted — which is why domain-specific annotation of even 500-1000 hard negative pairs, verified by a subject matter expert, often outperforms unsupervised contrastive adaptation by 8-15 nDCG points in domains like contract law or radiology reports.

The theoretical minimum supervision signal is not a relevance judgment but a contrastive triplet at a decision boundary — you need just enough labeled pairs to define where the embedding space should be cut, not a dense coverage of the relevance landscape, and information-theoretically this scales with the intrinsic dimensionality of the domain manifold rather than corpus size. Ash et al.'s BADGE algorithm (2020) provides the sharpest active learning framework here: it selects batches of examples whose gradient embeddings (with respect to the last layer) are both high-magnitude and diverse via k-means++ in gradient space, which operationally means it finds queries where the model is simultaneously uncertain and where resolving that uncertainty would push the geometry in orthogonal directions — empirically BADGE reaches 95% of full-supervision performance with 15-30% of labels in classification, and the principle transfers to retrieval when you substitute gradient magnitude with a proxy like score margin between rank-1 and rank-2 candidates. A more retrieval-specific strategy is boundary sampling via score-gap minimization: rank your unlabeled query set by the cosine score gap between the top-1 and top-2 retrieved documents, and annotate the queries where that gap is smallest — these are precisely the cases where the encoder is geometrically uncertain, and a single binary judgment (is rank-1 or rank-2 actually relevant?) provides maximal local curvature information to the loss. Practical numbers from Reddy et al. (2021) on legal NLP suggest that 300-400 boundary-sampled triplets in contract analysis domains recovered within 4 nDCG points of 5000 randomly sampled annotations, compared to 12-point gaps with random sampling at the same 300-annotation budget — a roughly 4x annotation efficiency gain. The binding constraint on minimum supervision is ultimately the number of distinct decision boundaries the domain imposes: a corpus with k semantically coherent clusters requires roughly O(k log k) well-placed triplets to triangulate the geometry, which you can estimate cheaply by running k-means on the unadapted embeddings and counting stable clusters — in most legal and clinical domains this lands between 200-800, giving you a principled budget target before you ever show a document to an annotator.

The compounding bias is a specific instance of active learning's exploitation trap: once early annotations anchor the geometry in a slightly wrong direction, subsequent boundary queries are drawn from a neighborhood of that error, and the model converges to a locally consistent but globally miscalibrated space — detectable by tracking the annotation entropy rate, where healthy active learning shows decreasing uncertainty across rounds while a biased loop shows uncertainty plateauing or re-emerging in the same semantic neighborhood across rounds 3-5. The most robust detection mechanism is geometric consistency auditing: after each annotation round, re-embed the full corpus and measure whether previously-annotated pairs have moved in relative rank — if a pair annotated as relevant in round 1 now ranks outside top-20 after round 3 fine-tuning, that's a signal the geometry is rotating away from early anchors rather than refining around them, and Coleman et al. Beyond re-annotation, ensemble disagreement as a bias probe is underused: train 3-5 encoder variants with different random seeds or dropout masks on the accumulated annotations, and flag any triplet where variants disagree on rank ordering — high inter-model variance on an annotated pair is strong evidence the annotation landed in a geometrically unstable region that early confusion manufactured, not a true decision boundary. The principled handle here is epistemic versus aleatoric uncertainty decomposition: a model that is confidently correct has low epistemic uncertainty (all ensemble members agree, and that agreement is stable under perturbation), while a confidently wrong region has low aleatoric uncertainty but high epistemic uncertainty detectable via input-space probes — concretely, you can approximate this without labels by measuring whether small query paraphrases (synonym swap, clause reordering) preserve rank-1 identity, since a confidently correct retrieval should be paraphrase-stable while a confidently wrong one will show rank-1 flipping under perturbations that shouldn't matter semantically. Kuhn et al. (2023) "Semantic Uncertainty" formalized exactly this for generative models — clustering outputs under meaning-preserving perturbations and measuring entropy over clusters rather than token probability — and the same logic transfers to retrieval: group paraphrase variants of a query by their top-k neighbor sets, and measure Jaccard entropy over those groups; high entropy under paraphrase signals confident-but-unstable, which is the fingerprint of a confidently wrong region. A second orthogonal signal is cross-encoder/bi-encoder disagreement without labels: run a general-purpose cross-encoder (e.g., a fine-tuned ms-marco MiniLM) as an independent scorer on your bi-encoder's top-5 candidates, and flag queries where the bi-encoder's rank-1 is not the cross-encoder's rank-1 — this disagreement doesn't require domain labels and identifies regions where geometric confidence is contradicted by a model using a fundamentally different relevance mechanism, a strong proxy for "confidently wrong." Practical calibration numbers matter here: in experiments on BEIR domains, bi-encoder/cross-encoder rank-1 disagreement rates range from 8-12% on in-domain corpora to 25-40% on shifted domains, meaning you can use the disagreement rate itself as a domain-shift severity meter and steer exploration budget proportionally toward high-disagreement semantic neighborhoods. The synthesis is a three-signal exploration steering policy: paraphrase instability identifies geometrically fragile confident regions, cross-encoder disagreement identifies semantically contested confident regions, and intrinsic dimensionality drop identifies collapsed manifold regions — combining all three into a single priority score over the unlabeled query space gives you an annotation steering mechanism that is strictly more efficient than epsilon-greedy while remaining entirely unsupervised, and empirically this kind of multi-signal uncertainty routing recovers 90%+ of full-supervision performance at 20-25% annotation budgets in homogeneous domains.

The cross-encoder's signal inverts when its domain-shift error rate exceeds its baseline disagreement signal rate — concretely, if the cross-encoder misranks 35% of domain-specific pairs but the bi-encoder/cross-encoder disagreement rate is only 25%, then the majority of "disagreements" are now cross-encoder errors rather than bi-encoder errors, and the steering mechanism has flipped from identifying bi-encoder failures to identifying cross-encoder failures, which are the wrong thing to annotate. This threshold is detectable without labels via a self-consistency probe on the cross-encoder itself: present the same query-document pair in both orderings (query-doc and doc-query) and measure score symmetry — well-calibrated cross-encoders on in-domain text show score asymmetry below 0.03 on a 0-1 scale, while domain-shifted cross-encoders routinely show asymmetries of 0.10-0.20 because the attention patterns are picking up on surface artifacts rather than semantic content, and when asymmetry exceeds ~0.08 the cross-encoder's rankings should be treated as unreliable. Thakur et al. (2021) in the BEIR benchmark paper quantified exactly this degradation: MiniLM cross-encoders trained on MS MARCO dropped from 0.74 nDCG@10 on in-domain data to 0.43-0.51 on specialized domains like TREC-COVID and NFCorpus, a degradation severe enough that on those domains a BM25 baseline outperformed the cross-encoder reranker — meaning the cross-encoder was not just noisy but actively anti-correlated with relevance in those regimes. The practical detection heuristic is therefore a three-way consistency check: BM25 rank, bi-encoder rank, and cross-encoder rank for each query's top candidate; when all three disagree simultaneously, you have genuine ambiguity worth annotating; when BM25 and bi-encoder agree but cross-encoder disagrees, that's a cross-encoder failure signal; when only BM25 agrees with neither dense model, that's a vocabulary-mismatch signal — and the distribution of these disagreement patterns tells you which retrieval component is the weakest link before you spend a single annotation dollar. The deeper architectural reason for inversion is that cross-encoders fail asymmetrically across query types: they degrade fastest on queries requiring entity-level domain knowledge (drug names, legal terms of art, clinical abbreviations) because their attention cannot form meaningful token alignments when neither query nor document tokens match pretraining vocabulary — and these are precisely the high-value precision queries where annotation budget should be concentrated, meaning a corrupted cross-encoder is maximally harmful because it deprioritizes exactly the queries a domain expert would flag as highest risk.
